title: Plant Migration
summary: Josh and Chuck (labeled as iHeart Intro in the transcript) discuss plant migration: how plants spread via spores and seeds (wind, animal, and water dispersal), fern spore travel, Clement's paradox of rapid plant migration (1899), studying migration through fossil pollen, permanent vegetation plots, and Alexander von Humboldt's Chimborazo records revisited by a 2012 Danish team. They cover the Green Sahara periods, post-glacial migration in North America after the Laurentide Glacier, climate change pushing trees poleward and upslope (University of Vermont red oak study, Purdue study of 86 eastern US tree species), community breakup, soil constraints, sugar maples in Quebec, boreal forest albedo feedback, tropical zones expanding northward, and assisted migration (assisted range expansion vs. assisted species migration, Monterey pine in Australia). The episode ends with a listener mail about the NATO phonetic alphabet and numbers, and a sign-off.
topics: Clement's paradox of rapid plant migration
University of Vermont red oak study

segments.title: Opening banter about ferns
segments.summary: The hosts open with banter about ferns, joking about a fern forest and where ferns come from.

segments.title: Fern spore travel and plant mobility
segments.summary: Josh gives stats on how far Tasmanian tree fern spores can travel (500 to 800 km) and how many spores a frond produces. He explains ferns as pioneer plants and that plant species can migrate even though individual plants are sessile.

segments.title: Oak migration and fast-spreading plants
segments.summary: The hosts discuss how fast-migrating plants produce spores or seeds young and disperse them far. Oaks spread slowly by gravity, but fossil records show faster movement.

segments.title: Detour on celebrity trivia
segments.summary: A digression about Anders Sandberg and Andy Samberg and their marriages, a tangent unrelated to plants.

segments.title: Clement's paradox of rapid plant migration
segments.summary: Clement's 1899 paradox describes trees migrating much faster than expected, such as after the last glacial period. Explanations include unusual weather or animals carrying seeds. The hosts name zoochory, anemochory, and hydrochory as dispersal modes.

segments.title: Studying plant migration: fossils, vegetation plots, and Humboldt
segments.summary: Methods include fossil records, permanent vegetation plots dating to about 1920, and historical journals. In 2012 a Danish team retraced Humboldt's Chimborazo trip and found species had moved up the mountain by about 500 meters on average.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the next segment.

segments.title: Satellite imagery and the Green Sahara
segments.summary: Satellite images are another short-term study method. Green Sahara periods allowed humans and wildlife to move and created mixed biomes, recurring about every 23,000 years.

segments.title: Post-glacial migration in North America
segments.summary: After the Laurentide Glacier retreated, it left bare ground that plants colonized. Southern trees trapped below the glacier later moved north as climate changed.

segments.title: Climate change rate versus plant migration
segments.summary: The hosts compare the rate of warming to the rate of plant migration. Earth warmed about 1.8 degrees Fahrenheit in 200 years, far faster than the roughly one degree per 1,400 years after the last glacial period.

segments.title: Who is faster: trees or climate
segments.summary: University of Vermont red oaks move about 0.1 to 0.3 miles per year while climate moves about 4 to 6 miles per year. A Purdue study of 86 eastern US tree species found hardwoods moving west and softwoods moving north.
topics: University of Vermont red oak study

segments.title: Community breakup and changing forest networks
segments.summary: Species move at different rates, breaking apart plant communities. Beech and hemlock are given as examples, and fossil pollen scientists say communities have always been unstable.

segments.title: Trapped trees and invasive species
segments.summary: Trees moving upslope can get squeezed into narrow bands when soils are poor. Gaps in community formation can let invasive species in.

segments.title: Sugar maples, boreal forests, and albedo feedback
segments.summary: Sugar maples are migrating north into Canada but struggle in Quebec's boreal soil. Replacement by grasses or weeds reduces carbon capture. Boreal forests are darker than ice and absorb more heat, creating a positive feedback loop.

segments.title: Tropical zones moving north and kill frost
segments.summary: Warming lets tropical zones expand; Florida and the southern US may become tropical by the end of the century. Fewer kill frosts means tropical plants can move north. Hosts discuss the term kill frost and a Dungeon Synth band named Kill Frost.

segments.title: Music tangent
segments.summary: The hosts talk about the band Destroyer, the New Pornographers, and the dungeon synth genre.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Break before the assisted migration discussion.

segments.title: Assisted migration and its three types
segments.summary: Humans helping plants migrate is called assisted migration. Its supporters argue doing nothing is worse. The three types are forest-assisted migration, assisted range expansion (within a plausible range), and assisted species migration (outside the range, considered riskiest).

segments.title: Monterey pine in Australia
segments.summary: The Monterey pine is native to California and endangered there but is an invasive weed in Australia, where it is pulled out in New South Wales and Victoria.

segments.title: Off-topic banter about accents and ringtones
segments.summary: The hosts talk about a New Zealand GPS voice saying rye, digital sounds, and ringtones. They close the topic with a joke about palm trees in New Mexico.

segments.title: Listener mail: NATO phonetic alphabet numbers
segments.summary: Listener William Lloyd (signed Tailwinds Decker), a pilot and former Air Force member, notes that the NATO alphabet includes number pronunciations like niner, tree, fower, and fife, which the hosts respond to.

segments.title: Sign-off and mail address
segments.summary: Hosts discuss a friend's email sign-off and invite listeners to send mail to the show's address.
